content:
The night the body turned up in the Limmat was one of those Zurich evenings where the rain drips like secrets down the cobblestones. I'd been sipping ersatz coffee at the Café Europa, lost in the haze of stale tobacco and regret, when the call came—a woman's scream, thick as a wet blanket. I grabbed my trench coat and stepped into the rain.

The body was a vision. A woman, no more than thirty, face splayed open like a flower the city had crushed. The Limmat took her blood like a thief, a dark ribbon running downstream. Her eyes looked like they'd been crying diamonds. I didn't know who she was then, but by morning, the streets of Zurich knew. They called her 'The Limmat Lady.' And I was the only man seeing her face while the others saw only the river.
